title: Pediatric Hypertension: AAP 2017 Blood Pressure Percentiles, Staging and Therapy
subject: ss-paediatric-nephrology

steps.say: Blood pressure classification in young children relies on normative percentiles based on age, sex, and height.
steps.tx: Apply established criteria for **AAP 2017 staging definitions (age 1-13 years)** during clinical screening. For children aged 1-13 years, blood pressure is categorized using normative percentile tables adjusted for age, sex, and height: Normal BP is < 90th percentile; Elevated BP is >= 90th to < 95th percentile (or 120/80 mmHg, whichever is lower); Stage 1 hypertension is >= 95th to < 95th percentile + 12 mmHg; and Stage 2 hypertension is >= 95th percentile + 12 mmHg (or >= 140/90 mmHg).

vis.title: AAP 2017 Blood Pressure Staging (Ages 1-13 Years)
rows: Confirm over 3 visits, ABPM, lifestyle + meds

steps.say: Beginning at thirteen years of age, pediatric staging aligns directly with adult guidelines using absolute thresholds.
steps.tx: Utilize simplified cutoffs for **Adolescent BP classification (age >= 13 years)** in older teenagers. In adolescents >= 13 years of age, the AAP guidelines align staging directly with the adult ACC/AHA definitions using absolute numerical thresholds: Normal BP is < 120/< 80 mmHg; Elevated BP is 120-129/< 80 mmHg; Stage 1 hypertension is 130-139/80-89 mmHg; and Stage 2 hypertension is >= 140/>= 90 mmHg.

steps.say: Twenty-four-hour ambulatory monitoring distinguishes true sustained hypertension from white-coat and masked phenotypes.
steps.tx: Order specialized testing with **Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) gold standard** protocols. Twenty-four-hour ABPM is the gold standard diagnostic tool to confirm persistent pediatric hypertension, assess nocturnal dipping, and reliably distinguish true sustained hypertension from white-coat hypertension (elevated in-clinic BP but normal ABPM) and masked hypertension (normal clinic BP but elevated wake or sleep mean BP > 95th percentile or abnormal BP load > 25%).

vis.title: Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring Phenotypes
rows: High risk; equal to sustained HTN

steps.say: Hypertension in children younger than six years is overwhelmingly secondary to renal parenchymal and vascular anomalies.
steps.tx: Prioritize diagnostic investigations based on **Etiology age stratification (secondary vs primary)** patterns. In young children < 6 years of age, hypertension is almost universally secondary (> 85%), most commonly caused by renal parenchymal diseases (such as CAKUT, glomerulonephritis, and reflux nephropathy), renovascular stenosis, or aortic coarctation; conversely, in post-pubertal adolescents, primary (essential) hypertension associated with obesity and metabolic syndrome predominates.

right.title: Adolescents >= 13 Years: Primary
points: Positive family history of essential hypertension
Milder Stage 1 elevations without organ damage
Absence of secondary historical or physical cues

steps.say: Echocardiographic assessment of left ventricular mass identifies early cardiac target organ damage.
steps.tx: Evaluate cardiac target-organ damage via **Left ventricular hypertrophy screening** at the time of diagnosis. Transthoracic echocardiography is indicated in all children with confirmed persistent hypertension to screen for hypertensive cardiomyopathy; left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) is formally defined as an elevated left ventricular mass index >= 38.6 g/m^2.7 for children and adolescent girls, or > 51 g/m^2.7 for adolescent boys, serving as a mandatory indication to initiate antihypertensive medication.

vis.title: Echocardiographic Target Organ Thresholds
rows: Indicates concentric or eccentric LV hypertrophy

steps.say: First-line pharmacological options comprise angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, receptor blockers, and calcium channel blockers.
steps.tx: Prescribe initial pharmacotherapy selecting from **First-line antihypertensive drug classes** recommended by pediatric guidelines. Acceptable first-line monotherapy classes in children include ACE inhibitors (such as enalapril or lisinopril), angiotensin receptor blockers (such as losartan), and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (such as amlodipine at 0.1-0.6 mg/kg/day once daily); thiazide diuretics are typically added as a second agent if monotherapy fails to achieve target blood pressure.

nodes.label: Stage 1 with LVH or Stage 2 Hypertension
Start ACEi (Enalapril), ARB (Losartan), or CCB (Amlodipine 0.1-0.6 mg/kg/day)
Inadequate response: Add Thiazide diuretic or second agent

steps.say: Severe blood pressure elevations accompanied by acute end-organ damage constitute a medical emergency.
steps.tx: Distinguish life-threatening presentations based on the **Hypertensive emergency vs urgency definition**. A hypertensive emergency is defined as severe Stage 2 hypertension (blood pressure > 30 mmHg above the 95th percentile or > 180/120 mmHg) accompanied by acute, life-threatening target-organ injury such as hypertensive encephalopathy, seizures, papilledema, acute pulmonary edema, aortic dissection, or acute renal failure, necessitating ICU admission and continuous intravenous infusions of nicardipine or labetalol.

left.title: Hypertensive Urgency
points: Managed with oral agents over 24-48 hours

right.title: Hypertensive Emergency
points: Acute encephalopathy, seizures, or heart failure

steps.say: Blood pressure must be lowered gradually to prevent watershed cerebral ischemia and neurological deficits.
steps.tx: Enforce strict guidelines regarding the **Rate of BP reduction in emergency** resuscitation. In a pediatric hypertensive emergency, rapid blood pressure reduction is strictly avoided to prevent ischemic cerebral or spinal infarction from loss of autoregulation; blood pressure should be lowered by no more than 25% of the planned reduction in the first 8 hours, followed by gradual normalization toward the 95th percentile over the subsequent 24-48 hours.

nodes.label: First 8 hours: Reduce BP by no more than 25% of excess
Next 24-48 hours: Gradually normalize toward 95th percentile
